analysis.one_liner: Repeals the corporate alternative minimum tax that large corporations must pay.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the corporate alternative minimum tax was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The corporate alternative minimum tax is a second tax calculation that corporations run alongside the regular tax; if the regular rules would let them pay little or nothing, they pay the minimum amount instead. This bill would have repealed that tax entirely, so large corporations that currently owe it would pay less. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be large, profitable corporations that owe the alternative minimum tax — often those with big deductions from depreciation, tax credits, or other preferences that reduce their regular tax bill. They would pay less in federal taxes. The federal government would collect less revenue, which would either raise deficits or shift costs to other taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large corporations that owe the minimum tax

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the corporate alternative minimum tax for all taxable years after enactment, eliminating the parallel tax corporations must compute under section 55 of the Internal Revenue Code [S3].
The CRS summary describes the bill as amending the Internal Revenue Code to repeal the corporate alternative minimum tax [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the cost, since repealing the minimum tax eliminates the payments corporations currently owe under it. That revenue shortfall would be made up through larger deficits or higher taxes on other taxpayers. Small businesses generally do not owe the corporate alternative minimum tax, so they would see no direct benefit.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the minimum tax removes the backstop designed to ensure that profitable corporations pay at least some federal tax even when deductions and credits reduce their regular tax liability to little or nothing, reducing federal revenue [S2] [S3].
The bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions — it simply terminates the tax — so the full cost of repeal would add to the deficit unless other taxes were raised elsewhere [S3].

Only large corporations with substantial tax preferences pay the corporate alternative minimum tax, so the benefits would flow to a concentrated set of large firms rather than broadly to businesses or households.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are concentrated on large corporations with enough deductions and credits to owe the minimum tax, while the cost falls on the federal treasury and, ultimately, on other taxpayers through deficits or shifted burdens. Supporters would argue the minimum tax adds complexity and distorts investment decisions; opponents would point out that it exists precisely to keep profitable corporations from paying nothing. On its own terms, this bill is a targeted tax cut for a concentrated interest with no offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the bill in the Senate on January 21, 1997 [S1].
On the same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 105th Congress, which ended January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death, but the federal treasury kept the revenue from the corporate minimum tax, and large corporations continued owing it rather than receiving the repeal. Because the bill was limited to one sponsor and two cosponsors and never advanced, its failure reflects limited support as much as committee inaction.

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. William Roth (R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, but the Republican-chaired Finance Committee also never advanced the bill.

industries.industry: Large corporations owing the alternative minimum tax
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the minimum tax these corporations owe, letting companies with large deductions and credits pay less in federal tax. The revenue lost would be borne by the federal treasury and other taxpayers.
Repeal would have eliminated a parallel tax computation that requires extensive corporate compliance work, a cost borne by the corporations themselves.
